Claude Code redirected to a rogue endpoint via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN env var AIInstallation Medium
Hunts persistent user-environment registry values that repoint Claude Code (or any Anthropic SDK client) away from Anthropic to a third-party gateway. Poison Claude explicitly instructs customers to set these variables so the CLI uses its relay instead of api.anthropic.com; a BASE_URL that isn't an Anthropic host, or any value referencing the known relay domains, is the enabling config for prompt exfiltration. Rationale: Uses the exact env-var names the Poison Claude onboarding instructs customers to set (confirmed via Requesty/Anthropic env-var docs) plus a non-anthropic.com BASE_URL condition and the relay-domain IOCs. The env var persists in HKCU\Environment, giving a durable registry pivot distinct from the network UC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/poison-claude-sells-discounted-claude.html • https://www.requesty.ai/blog/claude-code-environment-variables-anthropic-base-url-auth-token • https://developer.konghq.com/cookbooks/claude-code-sso/
ATT&CKT1112 T1567
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned internal LLM gateway (LiteLLM, Kong AI Gateway, Requesty, corporate proxy) legitimately setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an internal host
  • Developer pointing Claude Code at a self-hosted/on-prem Anthropic-compatible endpoint on an RFC1918 address
  • AWS Bedrock users (note: Bedrock uses CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK, not BASE_URL — should not match, but mixed configs exist)
  • QA/test automation setting the variable to a mock endpoint on localhost
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has "://localhost" or RegistryValueData has "://127.0.0.1" or RegistryValueData matches regex @"://(10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the RegistryValueData — is the endpoint an approved internal gateway, localhost/RFC1918, or an external/unknown host? Cross-check the setting user and whether the host also shows egress from UC1. 2) Contain: if the endpoint is external and unsanctioned, clear the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL/AUTH_TOKEN values, block the endpoint, and rotate any Anthropic/AWS Bedrock keys the user provisioned. 3) Hunt: sweep all dev endpoints for the same env-var names pointing off-Anthropic, check ~/.claude/settings.json for an equivalent 'env' override, and correlate with UC1 relay-domain egress to scope how many prompts were routed through the proxy.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Environment"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL","ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL" and RegistryValueData !has "anthropic.com" and isnotempty(RegistryValueData))
      or RegistryValueData has_any ("claudeopus.shop","bitsender.top","ecomagent.in")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "\\Environment"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL","ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
| where (RegistryValue =~ "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL" and RegistryValueData !has "anthropic.com" and isnotempty(RegistryValueData))
      or RegistryValueData has_any ("claudeopus.shop","bitsender.top","ecomagent.in")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Anthropic SDK Redirected via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL Environment Variable to Non-Anthropic Host
id: b71c0e94-2a55-4d18-9f6c-0c3d8e1a4b77
description: Detects a persistent user-environment registry value that points ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at a non-Anthropic endpoint or references the Poison Claude relay domains, redirecting Claude Code prompts to an attacker-controlled proxy.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/poison-claude-sells-discounted-claude.html
  - https://www.requesty.ai/blog/claude-code-environment-variables-anthropic-base-url-auth-token
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1112
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1567
logsource:
  category: registry_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_key:
    TargetObject|contains: '\Environment\'
    TargetObject|endswith:
      - 'ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL'
      - 'ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN'
      - 'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'
  selection_ioc:
    Details|contains:
      - 'claudeopus.shop'
      - 'bitsender.top'
      - 'ecomagent.in'
  filter_legit:
    Details|contains: 'anthropic.com'
  condition: selection_key and (selection_ioc or not filter_legit)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\\Environment\\ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL OR *\\Environment\\ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN OR *\\Environment\\ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OR *\\environment\\ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/ANTHROPIC_(BASE_URL|AUTH_TOKEN|API_KEY)/i
| CommandLine=/(claudeopus\.shop|bitsender\.top|ecomagent\.in)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Environment*" Registry.registry_value_name IN ("ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL","ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data 
| `drop_dm_object_name("Registry")` 
| search (registry_value_name="ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL" AND NOT registry_value_data="*anthropic.com*") OR registry_value_data IN ("*claudeopus.shop*","*bitsender.top*","*ecomagent.in*") 
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) 
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Environment*" Registry.registry_value_name IN ("ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL","ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data 
| `drop_dm_object_name("Registry")` 
| search (registry_value_name="ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL" AND NOT registry_value_data="*anthropic.com*") OR registry_value_data IN ("*claudeopus.shop*","*bitsender.top*","*ecomagent.in*") 
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) 
| sort - lastTime
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

Paperclip AI Flaws Let Attackers Run Host Commands via Malicious Agent Imports

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 9 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Two security flaws in Paperclip could let attackers execute commands on a network server or a developer's computer. Paperclip is an open-source control plane for teams of artificial intelligence (AI) agents, and both paths rely on importing a malicious agent and starting it. A third flaw could expose sensitive data and control-plane details through application programming interface (API) routes

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Paperclip AI process adapter spawning an interactive shell (host command execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Paperclip AI process adapter spawning an interactive shell (host command execution) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the terminal impact of CVE-2026-41679 and GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7: Paperclip's built-in process adapter launching an attacker-supplied command as a child of the server process. Pivots on a Paperclip parent context spawning a shell/LOLBin, which is the article's stated 'run host commands' outcome after a malicious agent import + wakeup. Rationale: Uses the article's stated behaviour that Paperclip's 'built-in process adapter intentionally launches a configured command as a child process of the server' and pivots parent context on the product name 'paperclip' with shell/recon children — the concrete host-command-execution endpoint of both critical chains. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-41679 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Paperclip agent legitimately configured with a process adapter that runs a shell wrapper or curl-based health check
  • DevOps sysadmin running Paperclip interactively from a shell whose command line still contains the 'paperclip' path
  • CI/CD job invoking the Paperclip CLI which then shells out to a build script
  • Legitimate agent that uses curl/wget to fetch data as its designed task
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("health","heartbeat","--version") and FileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine; confirm whether the shell/LOLBin maps to a sanctioned agent definition or is ad-hoc recon (whoami, id, cat /etc/passwd, curl to unknown host). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, stop the Paperclip service, and rotate the service-account credentials, board API tokens, and any secrets reachable to the agent process. 3) Hunt: check for a preceding .paperclip.yaml import and CLI-challenge self-approval, and confirm Paperclip is >= v2026.416.0; review new-company imports and open-registration accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "paperclip" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "paperclip"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","pwsh","sh","bash","zsh","dash","whoami","curl","curl.exe","wget")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "paperclip" or ParentProcessName has "paperclip"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","zsh","dash","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","whoami","curl","wget")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Paperclip AI Process Adapter Spawning a Shell
id: 6b7a1d2e-0f3c-4a91-9d51-8e2c4a5b7c10
description: Detects Paperclip AI server (process adapter) spawning an interactive shell or recon LOLBin, the host-command-execution impact of CVE-2026-41679 / GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7.
references:
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-41679
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/paperclip-ai-flaws-let-attackers-run.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'paperclip'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/dash'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentCommandLine:*paperclip* @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\whoami.exe OR *\curl.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentCommandLine=/paperclip/i
| ImageFileName=/(\/(sh|bash|zsh|dash)|\\cmd\.exe|\\powershell\.exe|\\pwsh\.exe|\/(whoami|curl|wget))$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","zsh","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","whoami","curl","wget") AND Processes.parent_process="*paperclip*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Malicious .paperclip.yaml agent-import bundle written to a Paperclip host AIDelivery Medium
Detects creation of the .paperclip.yaml bundle used in both CVE-2026-41679 and the DNS-rebinding chain to define a new company plus a process-adapter agent and its command. This is the delivery artifact an unauthorized or browser-originated import drops before the wakeup call triggers host execution. Rationale: Keys on the exact article-named artifact '.paperclip.yaml bundle defining a new company, an agent using the process adapter, and the command that agent would run' — a concrete, high-fidelity filename that precedes host execution. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-41679 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate operator authoring or updating a .paperclip.yaml during normal deployment/configuration
  • Version-control checkout (git) restoring a tracked .paperclip.yaml into a repo working directory
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Chef) templating out a sanctioned .paperclip.yaml
  • Developer testing a new agent locally in local_trusted mode
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","git","ansible","code.exe","Code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the .paperclip.yaml and inspect for a process-adapter agent plus an embedded command; identify the writing process (browser vs Paperclip service vs editor) and the account. 2) Contain: if the bundle defines a new company with a shell/command agent from an unexpected writer, quarantine the file, stop the Paperclip service before any wakeup, and block the source. 3) Hunt: correlate to a subsequent Paperclip-parent shell spawn (UC1), review web logs for the import + wakeup sequence, and enumerate recently created companies and self-approved board CLI credentials.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ ".paperclip.yaml"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".paperclip.yaml"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Paperclip Malicious Agent Import Bundle (.paperclip.yaml) Written
id: c1f2a3b4-5d6e-4789-a012-3b4c5d6e7f80
description: Detects creation of a .paperclip.yaml import bundle, the malicious new-company/process-adapter agent definition used in CVE-2026-41679 and GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7.
references:

  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/paperclip-ai-flaws-let-attackers-run.html

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DNS-rebinding to loopback against local_trusted Paperclip (external hostname resolving to 127.0.0.1) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7 browser->localhost crossing: an attacker-controlled hostname resolving to 127.0.0.1 so a browser's same-origin requests reach a loopback-bound Paperclip in local_trusted mode. Surfaces DNS answers and browser connections where a public FQDN maps to the loopback interface. Rationale: Encodes the article's DNS-rebinding mechanism verbatim: an attacker hostname 'resolved to both the attacker's server and 127.0.0.1' so later requests reach the local Paperclip service — flagged as a public FQDN resolving/connecting to loopback, which is anomalous outside this attack class. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/paperclip-ai-flaws-let-attackers-run.html
ATT&CKT1189 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Local dev tooling using a custom /etc/hosts or *.localtest.me / *.lvh.me style domain that resolves to 127.0.0.1 for HTTPS-on-localhost workflows
  • Container/dev frameworks (e.g. some Docker/mkcert setups) mapping a project FQDN to loopback
  • Split-horizon DNS or a captive-portal appliance briefly answering a public name with 127.0.0.1
  • Ad/tracker-blocking DNS (Pi-hole/hosts sinkhole) that null-routes domains to 127.0.0.1
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith "localtest.me" or RemoteUrl endswith "lvh.me" or RemoteUrl endswith ".test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving FQDN and the browser/host; determine whether the loopback answer comes from a sanctioned dev domain or a sinkhole vs an unfamiliar external domain. 2) Contain: if unexplained, capture the page/domain, block it at DNS/proxy, and confirm any loopback Paperclip is upgraded to v2026.416.0 (private-hostname guard enabled) so rebound Host headers are rejected. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for a following .paperclip.yaml import (UC2) and Paperclip-parent shell spawn (UC1), and review any local Paperclip access logs for imports/wakeup calls carrying the attacker hostname in the Host header.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl !in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1","::1")
| where RemoteUrl contains "."
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox.exe","firefox","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","Safari","Google Chrome")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where isnotempty(DstHostname)
| where DstHostname !in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1","::1")
| where DstHostname contains "."
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Rebinding to Loopback (Public Hostname Resolving to 127.0.0.1)

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

references:

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-41679")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-41679")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;

| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized npm Packages Employ NullReceiver Tactic to Decode C2 IP from Blockchain

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 10 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged an evolution of the EtherHiding blockchain-based command-and-control (C2) technique that conceals the C2 server IP address inside a made-up destination address of a completely empty Ethereum transfer. The new dead drop resolver approach, observed in two trojanized npm packages "bianira-ui" and "fluid-type-ui," has been codenamed NullReceiver by

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.002 T1566 T1566.002
IPs166.88.134.62

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Install of trojanized npm packages bianira-ui / fluid-type-ui
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] NullReceiver npm C2 beacon to hardcoded IP 166.88.134.62 · [LLM] NullReceiver dead-drop: node queries Ethereum RPC then beacons to a raw IP · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
NullReceiver npm C2 beacon to hardcoded IP 166.88.134.62 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host connecting outbound to 166.88.134.62, the C2 server that the trojanized npm packages bianira-ui and fluid-type-ui decode from the recipient bytes (a6 58 86 3e) of a zero-value Ethereum transfer. Because the packages impersonate front-end Tailwind/CSS UI libraries, a node process reaching this raw IP is unambiguously malicious. Rationale: 166.88.134.62 is a hardcoded network IOC confirmed by three independent write-ups (cybersecuritynews, gbhackers, cyberpress) and the OpenSourceMalware decode flowchart, giving it near-zero false-positive risk as a direct-match alert. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/north-korean-hackers-hiding-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/nullreceiver-wallet-trail/ • https://cyberpress.org/nullreceiver-hides-ethereum-c2/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal asset legitimately assigned 166.88.134.62 after attacker infrastructure is sinkholed/reassigned (verify current WHOIS/ASN)
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample intentionally
  • Threat-intel proxy or TAXII feed proactively probing the IOC
  • NAT egress where the IP is a shared upstream (rare for a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessCommandLine/process — expect node.exe/npm; pull the host's node_modules for bianira-ui or fluid-type-ui and the developer/user who ran the install. 2) Contain: block 166.88.134.62 at the egress firewall/EDR, isolate the host, and revoke any developer/CI credentials and npm tokens that lived on the box (DPRK Contagious Interview targets dev secrets). 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints and CI runners for outbound hits to this IP and for the two package names, and pivot on the attacker wallet 0xa322e5f3d311d3080e6f0121063e9adc2490ef1a to enumerate rotated C2 IPs.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "166.88.134.62"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "166.88.134.62"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DstHostname, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Install of trojanized npm packages bianira-ui / fluid-type-ui AIInstallation High
Hunts file writes into node_modules for the two known-malicious packages bianira-ui (by npmuser1101) and fluid-type-ui (by npmuser3002), which masquerade as Tailwind CSS plugins. Catches the supply-chain foothold at install time on developer workstations and CI runners regardless of the C2 IP, which rotates. Rationale: Package names bianira-ui and fluid-type-ui are corroborated by the original THN report plus cybersecuritynews and gbhackers; matching the node_modules install path yields a high-fidelity, IP-rotation-resistant detection that fires on the supply-chain foothold itself. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/north-korean-hackers-hiding-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/nullreceiver-wallet-trail/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package coincidentally named with the same string in an unrelated scoped path (unlikely given exact names)
  • Security team intentionally st[ag]ing the sample in a malware lab
  • Internal mirror/Artifactory caching the withdrawn package for IR analysis
  • Developer restoring an old lockfile that still references the removed package
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installing user and whether the package reached a runtime (node/npm parent) versus only lockfile resolution; grab package.json/package-lock.json to see how it entered the dependency tree. 2) Contain: uninstall the package, isolate the host/CI runner, rotate npm tokens, SSH keys, cloud creds and wallet keys present on the box, and purge any internal registry cache copies. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (outbound to 166.88.134.62), search all lockfiles across repos for the two names, and check for other packages from npmuser1101 and npmuser3002.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\node_modules\\bianira-ui", "/node_modules/bianira-ui", "\\node_modules\\fluid-type-ui", "/node_modules/fluid-type-ui")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("node_modules\\bianira-ui", "node_modules/bianira-ui", "node_modules\\fluid-type-ui", "node_modules/fluid-type-ui")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NullReceiver dead-drop: node queries Ethereum RPC then beacons to a raw IP AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the NullReceiver resolution behaviour itself: a node/npm process contacts a public Ethereum RPC provider (to read the attacker wallet's last transaction) and, within 5 minutes on the same host, connects to a raw public IP with no DNS/hostname — the decoded C2. This survives C2-IP and wallet rotation and flags copycat packages the IOCs miss. Rationale: The OpenSourceMalware flowchart (null.png) confirms the sequence npm package -> public Ethereum ledger lookup -> connect to decoded raw IP; correlating a node RPC read with a same-host connection to a hostname-less public IP within 5 min captures the technique generically, catching rotated wallets/IPs that pure IOC rules miss. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/trojanized-npm-packages-decode-c2-ip.html • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhp2JlYxtO8ERLKOUQWEHhsEpf5fOczPAzfCYSUfZJCs4_O3vxIogUH1sH3pDS3TnpeQ9ctxXu0QVfTQTdt9I_BfsYl8SaF5cpY_wKimW9-tkgLOE4tYnUr7aSVDnM4d0CEMr4pYT5KiV-_mCYQMzC_vhwRQDTUunVBKiBKjgFiAPMs_A1TSBlWubYasQHK/s1700-e365/null.png
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/dapp or wallet-integration project whose node backend polls an Ethereum RPC then opens raw-IP peer connections
  • Blockchain indexer / node client (ethers.js, web3.js, hardhat) running in dev or CI
  • Crypto price-ticker or NFT tooling that reads on-chain data
  • P2P libraries (libp2p, IPFS) that dial peers by IP after a bootstrap lookup
Suppression filter
// Suppress known-good web3 projects by initiating command line / working dir
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("hardhat", "truffle", "ethers", "web3", "foundry", "ganache")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the node process's working directory and package.json — a UI/CSS-themed dependency (like Tailwind plugins) that touches Ethereum RPC is the tell; capture the raw IP it dialed. 2) Contain: block the decoded raw IP and the parent package, isolate the host, and rotate developer/CI secrets. 3) Hunt: enrich the raw IP against threat intel, pivot the host's process tree for the trojanized package names, and add the newly-observed C2 IP and any new attacker wallet addresses to the IOC watchlist for org-wide sweeping.
let LookbackDays = 30d;

let RpcHosts = dynamic(["mainnet.infura.io","eth-mainnet.g.alchemy.com","cloudflare-eth.com","rpc.ankr.com","ethereum.publicnode.com","api.etherscan.io","etherscan.io","eth.llamarpc.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","rpc.flashbots.net"]);
let BlockchainLookups = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm")
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (RpcHosts)
    | project RpcTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RpcHost = RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;

| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isempty(RemoteUrl)

| where Timestamp between (RpcTime .. RpcTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| project RpcTime, RawIpTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, RpcHost, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by RawIpTime desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

New OVSwrap Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Local Users Gain Root via Open vSwitch

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A memory corruption flaw in the Linux kernel's Open vSwitch datapath gives ordinary local users a path to root on a broad set of default-configured distributions, and a public exploit ships with pre-built records for roughly 800 kernel builds. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-64531 (CVSS score: 7.8) and codenamed OVSwrap by its discoverer, was disclosed by security researcher Asim

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] OVSwrap privesc: unprivileged `unshare -Urn` to obtain CAP_NET_ADMIN in new netns · [LLM] OVSwrap: openvswitch kernel module load/autoload on a host that doesn't run ovs-vswitchd · [LLM] OVSwrap AppArmor bypass: `aa-exec -p trinity` userns-restriction fallback (Ubuntu 24.04) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OVSwrap post-exploit: /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d modified outside package/config tooling · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New OVSwrap Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Local Users Gain Root via Open vSwitch
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
OVSwrap privesc: unprivileged `unshare -Urn` to obtain CAP_NET_ADMIN in new netns AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the OVSwrap (CVE-2026-64531) entry step where an ordinary local user runs `unshare -Urn` to create private user+network namespaces and gain CAP_NET_ADMIN inside them, the prerequisite for reaching the vulnerable Open vSwitch flow-installation path. This is the exact invocation the public PoC uses to start the chain on default-configured distros. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact PoC command `unshare -Urn` (creating user+network namespaces to gain CAP_NET_ADMIN); non-root actor excludes normal privileged container tooling. Corroborated against CloudLinux and securityonline write-ups of the same PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-mitigation/ • https://securityonline.info/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-local-root/ • https://cloudlinux.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/29223197225116-Kernel-Local-Privilege-Escalation-CVE-2026-64531-OVSwrap-Open-vSwitch-Affected-Status-and-Fix
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container runtimes (Podman/rootless Docker, LXC, bubblewrap) legitimately creating user+net namespaces
  • CI/CD sandboxing jobs using unshare for isolation
  • Developers testing network namespaces manually
  • Flatpak/snap application launches that spin up namespaces
  • nsenter/unshare used by systemd or debugging tooling
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("podman","dockerd","containerd","runc","lxc-start","bwrap","flatpak","snap","systemd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the unshare PID on the host — is the parent an interactive shell of a non-service user, and does an openvswitch module load or sudoers write follow within seconds? 2) Contain: if the actor is untrusted/multi-tenant, freeze the account, snapshot the host, and apply the module block `echo 'install openvswitch /bin/false' > /etc/modprobe.d/ovswrap.conf` then unload/reboot. 3) Hunt: search the same host and user for subsequent `modprobe/insmod openvswitch`, `aa-exec -p trinity`, and writes to /etc/sudoers* — confirming the OVSwrap chain vs. benign namespace usage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "unshare"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-Urn","-rUn","-Unr") or (ProcessCommandLine has "--user" and ProcessCommandLine has "--net" and (ProcessCommandLine has "--map-root-user" or ProcessCommandLine has "-r"))
| where AccountName != "root" and AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/unshare" or TargetProcessName == "unshare"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-Urn","-rUn") or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--user" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--net")
| where ActorUsername != "root"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OVSwrap CVE-2026-64531 Unprivileged unshare User+Net Namespace Creation
id: 6f2a9c14-7b3e-4d8a-9c1f-2a5e8d0b4c31
description: Detects the unshare -Urn invocation used by the OVSwrap PoC to gain CAP_NET_ADMIN in a private user+network namespace
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html
  - https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-mitigation/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.privilege_escalation
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '/unshare'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-Urn'
      - '-rUn'
  selection_longflags:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--user'
      - '--net'
  filter_root:
    User: 'root'
  condition: selection_img and (selection_flags or selection_longflags) and not filter_root
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:unshare (@process.command_line:*Urn* OR @process.command_line:*map\-root\-user*) -@user.id:0
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/unshare$/i
| regex("(-Urn|-rUn|--user.*--net)", field=CommandLine)
| UserName!=root
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=unshare (Processes.process="*-Urn*" OR Processes.process="*- Urn*" OR (Processes.process="*--user*" AND Processes.process="*--net*" AND (Processes.process="*--map-root-user*" OR Processes.process="* -r *"))) Processes.user!=root by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=unshare (Processes.process="*-Urn*" OR Processes.process="*- Urn*" OR (Processes.process="*--user*" AND Processes.process="*--net*" AND (Processes.process="*--map-root-user*" OR Processes.process="* -r *"))) Processes.user!=root by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
OVSwrap: openvswitch kernel module load/autoload on a host that doesn't run ovs-vswitchd AIExploitation Medium
Hunts loading of the vulnerable openvswitch datapath module via modprobe/insmod — the OVSwrap exploit triggers auto-load by resolving the Generic Netlink family name, so the module can appear even where lsmod was previously empty and ovs-vswitchd is not deployed. On non-OVS/OpenStack hosts this load is anomalous and a direct signal of CVE-2026-64531 exploitation prep. Rationale: Uses the article's specific module name `openvswitch` and the auto-load-by-genl-family behaviour it calls out; scoping to hosts that don't run ovs-vswitchd makes the module load high-signal. Confirmed as the exploited component in SentinelOne and CloudLinux advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-64531/ • https://cloudlinux.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/29223197225116-Kernel-Local-Privilege-Escalation-CVE-2026-64531-OVSwrap-Open-vSwitch-Affected-Status-and-Fix
ATT&CKT1547.006 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OpenStack / OVN / OVS hypervisor and network nodes loading openvswitch at boot
  • systemd-modules-load.service or /etc/modules-load.d loading OVS on networking hosts
  • Kubernetes CNI plugins (e.g. OVN-Kubernetes, Antrea) loading the datapath
  • Admin manually enabling Open vSwitch for a new bridge
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/Puppet) provisioning OVS on network infra
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in (dynamic(["ovs-node-01","ovs-node-02"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemd","systemd-modules-load","ansible","puppet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a legitimate OVS/OpenStack/OVN/CNI node (is ovs-vswitchd installed and enabled?). If not, treat the load as suspicious. 2) Contain: on non-OVS hosts, deploy `echo 'install openvswitch /bin/false' > /etc/modprobe.d/ovswrap.conf`, then unload the resident module (`modprobe -r openvswitch`) or schedule a reboot; isolate if multi-tenant. 3) Hunt: correlate a preceding `unshare -Urn` by a non-root user and any following /etc/sudoers* writes or new root shells on the same host to confirm the OVSwrap chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("modprobe","insmod","kmod")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "openvswitch"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Loads=count(),
            SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5)
            by DeviceName, AccountName, FileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/modprobe","/insmod","/kmod") or TargetProcessName in~ ("modprobe","insmod","kmod")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "openvswitch"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OVSwrap AppArmor bypass: `aa-exec -p trinity` userns-restriction fallback (Ubuntu 24.04) AIExploitation High
Detects the OVSwrap PoC's AppArmor bypass fallback — where direct namespace creation is blocked on Ubuntu 24.04, the exploit re-runs itself under the permissive `trinity` profile via `aa-exec -p trinity` to restore reachability to the vulnerable path. The `aa-exec -p trinity` string is a near-unique PoC artifact. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact PoC artifact `aa-exec -p trinity`, an AppArmor-confinement bypass specific to the OVSwrap exploit on Ubuntu 24.04 — extremely unlikely to appear in benign administration. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html • https://pbxscience.com/ovswrap-flaw-in-linux-kernels-open-vswitch-lets-local-users-become-root/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A site that legitimately ships a custom AppArmor profile literally named 'trinity'
  • Security researchers reproducing the OVSwrap PoC in an authorized lab
  • AppArmor profile testing/QA that invokes aa-exec with a named profile
  • Automated exploit-detection or vuln-scanning tooling replaying the PoC
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is near-unique to the PoC — immediately confirm the host, actor, and whether a 'trinity' AppArmor profile even legitimately exists there (`aa-status`). 2) Contain: isolate the host, freeze the invoking account, capture memory/process tree; on Ubuntu re-enable the userns AppArmor restriction and apply the openvswitch module block. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the full chain — preceding `unshare -Urn`, openvswitch module load, and following /etc/sudoers* modification or unexpected uid=0 shells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "aa-exec"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "trinity"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","--profile")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/aa-exec" or TargetProcessName == "aa-exec"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "trinity" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","--profile")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OVSwrap post-exploit: /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d modified outside package/config tooling AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OVSwrap PoC's post-root action — after corrupting a kernel credential it modifies /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers to entrench root access before opening a root shell. Flags writes to these paths by processes that are not the sanctioned sudoers editors or package/config-management tooling. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit post-exploit action — the PoC modifies /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers to persist root — and filters the known-good editors/package managers so only anomalous writers surface. Datadog left empty: the linux.auditd standard schema exposes process/user fields but not a reliable file-path attribute for this write. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-mitigation/
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef/Salt) deploying sudoers drop-ins
  • cloud-init seeding sudoers for a new cloud instance's default user
  • Admin adding a sudo rule via a text editor instead of visudo
  • Package post-install scripts dropping files into /etc/sudoers.d
  • IdM/SSSD or FreeIPA tooling syncing sudo rules
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("salt-minion","ansible","puppet","chef-client","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the newly written sudoers content and identify the writing process and user — a non-editor writer (e.g. an exploit binary or unexpected shell) adding NOPASSWD/ALL for a normal user is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: revert the sudoers change, revoke/reset the affected account, isolate the host and preserve the file plus process tree for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for the OVSwrap precursors — `unshare -Urn`, openvswitch module load, `aa-exec -p trinity` — and any root shell spawned immediately after the write; patch to a fixed vendor kernel.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath == "/etc/sudoers" or FolderPath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("visudo","sudoedit","apt","apt-get","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","puppet","chef-client","ansible","cloud-init","unattended-upgr")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath == "/etc/sudoers" or TargetFilePath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate","FileWrite")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("visudo","sudoedit","apt","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","puppet","chef-client","ansible","cloud-init"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Kali365 Weaponizes Microsoft Authentication Against US Companies: New Enterprise Risk

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 9 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Kali365 is turning a legitimate Microsoft login into a gateway to corporate data. The phishing kit targets US organizations with attacker-controlled device codes that victims approve on Microsoft's real authentication page. Once access and refresh tokens are issued, attackers may retain access to email, documents, and cloud resources, creating a direct path to data exposure, financial fraud,

ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566 T1566.002
Domainsbluefoodtruths.xyz flexiscalesystems.de guardedwebsolutions.de proforcstaffing.com reputationboosters.de guardextion.online prowebsitemakers.de onlinebrandinghub.de onsite-developments.net functionalityfirst.de
