Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Host or mailbox contact with Kali365 lure domains (SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign decoys) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kali365 device-code-flow authentication used by a standard M365 user · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Kali365 concurrent device-code sign-in: same user, 2+ IPs/countries in one hour · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Kali365 device-code-flow authentication used by a standard M365 user AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth device-code grant, which Kali365 abuses to have victims approve an attacker-generated code on Microsoft's real login page. Device-code flow is legitimate but rare for interactive knowledge workers, making its appearance on a normal user account a high-value pivot for token theft. Rationale: Uses the article's core TTP — attacker-controlled device codes approved on Microsoft's legitimate device-login portal — expressed as the OAuth device-code grant, which is the single defining signal of Kali365 token issuance. AuthenticationProtocol not being an available column in this tenant's SigninLogs schema, the flow is matched on the deviceCode marker inside AuthenticationDetails. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineers authenticating Azure CLI / Azure PowerShell on a shell that cannot pop a browser
  • Conference-room / Teams Rooms and smart-TV devices enrolling via device code
  • IoT or headless kiosk provisioning that legitimately uses the device-code grant
  • Developers logging into az login --use-device-code over SSH
  • New MDM/Intune device onboarding using device-code sign-in
Suppression filter
| where not (Application has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and DeviceTrustType == "Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the user's device-code sign-ins — check the resource/app requested, source IP geo, and whether the user owns a headless/CLI workflow that would explain it. Compare the sign-in IP to the user's normal locations. 2. Contain: if unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-MFA; block the source IP. 3. Hunt: enumerate all OAuth tokens/apps consented for the account, review mailbox rules and recent mail/file access, and search other users for device-code sign-ins from the same IP/ASN within 24h.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // device-code grant marker in the auth-detail JSON
| where ErrorCode == 0                            // completed sign-in => token issued
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(Country, 20),
            Apps = make_set(Application, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
            by AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // device-code grant marker in AuthenticationDetails JSON
| where ResultType == 0                           // successful sign-in
| where isnotempty(UserPrincipalName)
| extend CountryOrRegion = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(CountryOrRegion, 20),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
            by UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Kali365 Device Code Flow Authentication Success
id: 6f2b1c94-2e77-4a1d-9c5a-8b0d3f7e2a11
description: Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth device-code grant, abused by the Kali365 phishing kit for token theft.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1621
logsource:
  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  selection:
    AuthenticationProtocol: deviceCode
    ResultType: 0
  condition: selection
level: medium
CLOUD
sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" "properties.authenticationProtocol"="deviceCode" "properties.status.errorCode"=0
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values("properties.ipAddress") as ipAddress values("properties.appDisplayName") as app values("properties.resourceDisplayName") as resource dc("properties.ipAddress") as ipCount by user
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Kali365 concurrent device-code sign-in: same user, 2+ IPs/countries in one hour AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates successful device-code-flow sign-ins for a single user across two or more distinct IPs or countries within a one-hour window — the pattern seen when a victim approves the code from their location while the Kali365 operator uses the issued token from separate infrastructure. Adds temporal + geo divergence on top of the raw device-code signal to raise fidelity. Rationale: Builds on the article's device-code abuse by adding the operational tell that the person approving the code and the person using the resulting token are in different places — 2+ IPs/countries for the same user in a 1h device-code window. Correlation/threshold shape, so Sigma is intentionally omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Traveling user whose VPN egress and local carrier IP both appear within the hour
  • Mobile users roaming between Wi-Fi and cellular NAT pools mapped to different geos
  • Corporate proxy / cloud-egress that presents multiple regional IPs for one session
  • Legitimate CLI auth from a datacenter jump host while the user is also at their desk
  • Geo-IP database inaccuracy splitting a single ISP block across two countries
Response runbook
1. Triage: list the two+ IPs and their ASNs/geos for the flagged hour; determine which IP matches the user's known device/location and whether the other is a hosting/VPS provider (operator infra). 2. Contain: revoke refresh tokens and sessions for the account, force password reset + re-MFA, and add the non-user IP/ASN to conditional-access block. 3. Hunt: pivot on the suspicious IP across all users for device-code sign-ins, review the account's OAuth grants, inbox rules, and file/mail access since first-seen; check for token replay against Exchange/SharePoint from the same IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize IPs = dcount(IPAddress), Countries = dcount(Country),
            IPList = make_set(IPAddress, 20), CountryList = make_set(Country, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where IPs >= 2 or Countries >= 2   // victim approves locally, operator uses token from other infra
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == 0
| where isnotempty(UserPrincipalName)
| extend CountryOrRegion = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize IPs = dcount(IPAddress), Countries = dcount(CountryOrRegion),
            IPList = make_set(IPAddress, 20), CountryList = make_set(CountryOrRegion, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where IPs >= 2 or Countries >= 2   // victim approves locally, operator uses token from other infra
| order by LastSeen desc
CLOUD
sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" "properties.authenticationProtocol"="deviceCode" "properties.status.errorCode"=0
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc("properties.ipAddress") as ipCount dc("location.countryOrRegion") as countryCount values("properties.ipAddress") as ips values("location.countryOrRegion") as countries by user, _time
| where ipCount>=2 OR countryCount>=2
| sort - _time
Host or mailbox contact with Kali365 lure domains (SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign decoys) AIDelivery High
Matches endpoint web/DNS traffic and delivered email URLs against the confirmed Kali365 lure-hosting domains that impersonate SharePoint, OneDrive and DocuSign to funnel victims into the device-code flow. This is the earliest detectable stage — the lure/redirect — before any Microsoft token is issued. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the article's pre-extracted Kali365 lure domains — high fidelity because these are dedicated attacker-registered domains with no legitimate business use; catches the lure/redirect stage before a token is ever issued. Covers DNS, endpoint web egress, and mail-delivered URLs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst detonating the lure URL in a sandbox from a corporate endpoint
  • Threat-intel enrichment / URL-scanning tooling resolving the domains for feeds
  • A previously-benign domain being sinkholed and now resolving to a research IP
  • User forwarding the phishing mail internally causing repeated URL clicks by responders
  • Newly-parked domain reuse where the string collides with an unrelated legitimate host (validate WHOIS)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the user/device that resolved or browsed the domain and whether a device-code sign-in followed within the next 30 minutes (join to UC1 signal). Confirm the domain is still live/malicious. 2. Contain: block all 20 domains at proxy/DNS/firewall and quarantine the delivering email tenant-wide; if a sign-in followed, revoke the user's tokens and force MFA reset. 3. Hunt: search email, web and DNS across the org for any of the domains, expand to newly-registered look-alike SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign domains on the same registrar/ASN, and push the IOCs to SIEM/TIP for retrospective search.
let Kali365Domains = dynamic(["bluefoodtruths.xyz","flexiscalesystems.de","guardedwebsolutions.de","proforcstaffing.com","reputationboosters.de","guardextion.online","prowebsitemakers.de","onlinebrandinghub.de","onsite-developments.net","functionalityfirst.de","buildyouronlineidentity.de","flexievolve.de","onlineidentityperfection.de","guardwebsolutions.de","securedecisionmaking.de","modernwebbalance.de","marketadaptabletech.de","waschmaschinenmarkt.de","hbaknoxvillecom.top","brandswithintegrity.de"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (Kali365Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let Kali365Domains = dynamic(["bluefoodtruths.xyz","flexiscalesystems.de","guardedwebsolutions.de","proforcstaffing.com","reputationboosters.de","guardextion.online","prowebsitemakers.de","onlinebrandinghub.de","onsite-developments.net","functionalityfirst.de","buildyouronlineidentity.de","flexievolve.de","onlineidentityperfection.de","guardwebsolutions.de","securedecisionmaking.de","modernwebbalance.de","marketadaptabletech.de","waschmaschinenmarkt.de","hbaknoxvillecom.top","brandswithintegrity.de"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| extend UrlHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Url).Host))
| where UrlHost in (Kali365Domains)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical Gitea Flaw Let Unauthenticated Attackers Read Server Files via Org-Mode Markup

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An unauthenticated attacker can read any file the service account can access on Gitea, the self-hosted Git platform, in versions 1.22.1 through 1.27.0. No login, no repository write access. A public repository and crafted Org-mode markup are enough. The flaw is fixed in Gitea 1.27.1. The file-read flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-59774, rated Critical with a CVSS score of 9.8, and received its

CVEsCVE-2026-59774 CVE-2026-60004 CVE-2026-20896 CVE-2026-27771
ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566 T1566.002
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Anonymous POST to Gitea Org-mode markup endpoint (CVE-2026-59774 file-read) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gitea process spawning unexpected shell/tooling from a hook (CVE-2026-59774 token-to-hook escalation)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Anonymous POST to Gitea Org-mode markup endpoint (CVE-2026-59774 file-read) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated POST requests to Gitea's /{owner}/{repo}/markup rendering endpoint, the file-read primitive in CVE-2026-59774 where an Org-mode #+INCLUDE directive with an absolute path (Mode: file) coerces the vulnerable go-org ReadFile callback (ioutil.ReadFile) into returning arbitrary server files (e.g. app.ini and its INTERNAL_TOKEN) readable by the Gitea service account. Article-specific because it keys on the exact vulnerable route and the anonymous-access precondition against a public repo with the code unit enabled. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable route POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup plus the anonymous-user precondition the advisory names; scStatus 200 confirms the render succeeded. Request body (Mode: file / absolute path) isn't in access logs, so we alert on the endpoint+anon+success triad. Cross-checked against the Gitea advisory and go-gitea PR #38642/#38645 cited in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/38642 • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/38645 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59774
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated users using the Gitea web-UI live markdown/Org preview where the reverse proxy logs an empty/'-' username
  • External vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei) probing the markup route
  • Uptime/health-check bots POSTing to Gitea paths
  • CI integrations that render markup anonymously against public repos
  • Security researchers re-testing the patch after upgrade to 1.27.1
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "Qualys" and csUserAgent !has "Nessus" and csUserAgent !has "nuclei" and csUserAgent !has "Nmap"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target Gitea build is 1.22.1–1.27.0 (vulnerable) and that scStatus=200; pull the full request from the reverse proxy/WAF to see whether the POST body contains Org-mode '#+INCLUDE' with 'Mode: file' or an absolute path (e.g. app.ini). Note the source IP and repeat cadence. 2) Contain: upgrade to 1.27.1 immediately; block the offending source IP at the proxy; treat all secrets readable by the Gitea service account as exposed and rotate INTERNAL_TOKEN, OAuth material, JWT signing keys, and DB credentials. 3) Hunt: search hook directories under gitea-repositories for unexpected executables and pivot to UC 'Gitea process spawning unexpected interpreter' for the token→hook escalation.
// Gitea commonly fronted by IIS/nginx/WAF; this targets IIS W3C logs. For nginx use Syslog, for a WAF use CommonSecurityLog (RequestMethod/RequestURL/SourceUserName).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem endswith "/markup"
| where csUsername == "-" or isempty(csUsername)   // anonymous / unauthenticated
| where scStatus == 200
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, Computer, csMethod, csUriStem, csUsername, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea process spawning unexpected shell/tooling from a hook (CVE-2026-59774 token-to-hook escalation) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the escalation chain in CVE-2026-59774 where a leaked INTERNAL_TOKEN is used to inject a Git hook via the internal logger, then triggered during an anonymous clone. Detects the Gitea/git server process spawning an interpreter or network tool (bash, sh, python, perl, nc, curl, wget) whose command line references a hooks path, gitea-repositories, /tmp, or a /dev/tcp reverse shell — behaviour that does not occur during a normal read-only clone. Rationale: The advisory's escalation is INTERNAL_TOKEN -> injected hook -> triggered on anonymous clone; a read-only clone should never cause the Gitea server to spawn an interpreter or a /dev/tcp reverse shell. Keys on the gitea/git parent plus interpreter child plus hook/gitea-repositories/tmp/dev-tcp command-line context, excluding legit git-lfs/git-shell helpers. Chain is single-sourced to Gitea's advisory, hence hunting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/38642 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59774
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom server-side Git hooks (pre-receive/post-receive/update) that call curl or wget for CI/webhook notifications
  • git-lfs or git-shell helper processes spawned during push/pull
  • Admin maintenance or migration scripts operating under gitea-repositories
  • Backup jobs reading repo trees including hooks directories
  • Gitea internal hooks writing to /tmp during large-repo operations
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git-lfs","git-shell","git rev-list","git pack-objects"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the referenced hook file under gitea-repositories/<owner>/<repo>.git/hooks/ (or custom_hooks/); confirm the file is unexpected, recently created, and not part of a configured webhook. Correlate the host/time with UC1 anonymous /markup hits. 2) Contain: isolate the Gitea host, kill the process, quarantine the malicious hook file, and rotate INTERNAL_TOKEN/OAuth/JWT/DB credentials since a token leak precedes this stage; upgrade to 1.27.1. 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos' hook directories for other planted executables, review outbound connections from the gitea process for C2, and check for new admin users or SSH keys added post-compromise.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gitea","git")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","curl","wget")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hooks/","gitea-repositories","/tmp/","/dev/tcp")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "git-lfs" and ProcessCommandLine !has "git-shell"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("gitea","git")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","curl","wget")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hooks/","gitea-repositories","/tmp/","/dev/tcp")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "git-lfs" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "git-shell"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gitea Server Process Spawning Unexpected Interpreter from Hook Path (CVE-2026-59774 escalation)
id: b21d4c6e-8a17-4f3b-9c02-71e5a9d3f884
description: Detects the Gitea/git server process spawning a shell or network tool whose command line references a hook path, gitea-repositories, /tmp, or /dev/tcp - the token-to-hook command-execution escalation of CVE-2026-59774.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/critical-gitea-flaw-let-unauthenticated.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/gitea'
      - '/git'
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
  context:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hooks/'
      - 'gitea-repositories'
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/dev/tcp'
  condition: selection and context
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate custom Git server-side hooks invoking curl/wget for CI webhooks
  - git-lfs / git-shell helper invocations
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(bash OR sh OR dash OR python OR python3 OR perl OR nc OR ncat OR curl OR wget) (@process.command_line:(*hooks/* OR *gitea-repositories* OR */tmp/* OR */dev/tcp*)) -@process.command_line:(*git-lfs* OR *git-shell*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(gitea|git)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|dash|python3?|perl|nc|ncat|curl|wget)$/i
| regex("(hooks/|gitea-repositories|/tmp/|/dev/tcp)", field=CommandLine)
| NOT regex("(git-lfs|git-shell)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name=gitea OR Processes.parent_process_name=git) (Processes.process_name=bash OR Processes.process_name=sh OR Processes.process_name=dash OR Processes.process_name=python OR Processes.process_name=python3 OR Processes.process_name=perl OR Processes.process_name=nc OR Processes.process_name=ncat OR Processes.process_name=curl OR Processes.process_name=wget) (Processes.process="*hooks/*" OR Processes.process="*gitea-repositories*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(process, "git-lfs|git-shell|git rev-list|git pack-objects")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name=gitea OR Processes.parent_process_name=git) (Processes.process_name=bash OR Processes.process_name=sh OR Processes.process_name=dash OR Processes.process_name=python OR Processes.process_name=python3 OR Processes.process_name=perl OR Processes.process_name=nc OR Processes.process_name=ncat OR Processes.process_name=curl OR Processes.process_name=wget) (Processes.process="*hooks/*" OR Processes.process="*gitea-repositories*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

Leaked n8n API Tokens Exposed Live Instances to Credential Theft

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

GitGuardian researchers found 321 n8n instances accepting API tokens exposed in public GitHub commits and demonstrated four ways attackers could use them to access sensitive data and downstream credentials without exploiting a software vulnerability. We scanned public GitHub commits for exposed n8n API tokens and identified 4,576 unique credentials associated with 1,255 hostnames. Of the 896

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] n8n public API endpoint enumeration / credential-harvest fan-out from single source · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] n8n API key (X-N8N-API-KEY) exposed on command line or in Claude Code config on endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Leaked n8n API Tokens Exposed Live Instances to Credential Theft
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Authenticated n8n public REST API access to credential/user endpoints from external source
Authenticated n8n public REST API access to credential/user endpoints from external source AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts successful (HTTP 200) authenticated calls to n8n's public REST API sensitive endpoints (/api/v1/credentials, /api/v1/users) originating from a public/internet source IP. GitGuardian showed 321 live n8n instances accepted leaked JWT API tokens (passed via X-N8N-API-KEY) that let an attacker read stored-credential objects and user PII without any CVE. This targets the valid-token abuse directly on the instance's web tier. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact public-API paths (/api/v1/credentials, /api/v1/users) and the X-N8N-API-KEY auth model; a 200 to these endpoints from an external IP is the concrete signature of a leaked-token holder reading stored credentials/PII. Cross-checked GitGuardian's write-up and THN's CVE-2025-68613 KEV coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitguardian.com/n8n-security-encryption-key-compromise/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/cisa-flags-actively-exploited-n8n-rce.html
ATT&CKT1078 T1528 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal automation / CI job calling the n8n public API from a NAT egress IP that resolves as public
  • SaaS uptime/monitoring vendor polling the API endpoint
  • A partner integration authorized to read workflow credentials metadata
  • Security scanner / ASM tool crawling the exposed instance
  • n8n.cloud-hosted instance where all traffic is proxied and every SrcIpAddr looks external
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !startswith "n8n/"   // exclude internal n8n-to-n8n service calls
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SrcIpAddr + UserAgent; check whether the IP belongs to a sanctioned automation/monitoring egress or is unknown/hosting-provider/Tor. Confirm which token (jti) authenticated by correlating n8n audit logs. 2) Contain: in n8n Settings > API, revoke/delete the offending API key(s) and rotate N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY plus every stored credential the account could reference; block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: search GitHub/org repos for the leaked token and hostname pattern (N8N_API_KEY, .claude/settings.json), review /api/v1/executions and workflow-create calls from the same IP for credential-exfil workflows, and check for follow-on CVE-2025-68613 expression-injection attempts.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/v1/"
| where Url has_any ("/api/v1/credentials", "/api/v1/users")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))   // leaked-token abuse arrives from arbitrary internet IPs
| summarize Reqs=count(), Endpoints=make_set(Url, 20), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by Reqs desc
title: n8n Public API Access to Sensitive Endpoints
id: b3f1c7a2-2d94-4e61-9a3c-7f0e5c1d8a44
description: Detects HTTP GET access to n8n public REST API credential and user endpoints, associated with leaked X-N8N-API-KEY token abuse.

  - https://blog.gitguardian.com/n8n-security-encryption-key-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:

  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1213

  category: webserver

  selection:
    cs-method: GET
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/api/v1/credentials'

    sc-status: 200

WEB

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/*" (Web.url="*/api/v1/credentials*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/users*") Web.status=200 Web.http_method=GET by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_user_agent Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) AND NOT cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/*" (Web.url="*/api/v1/credentials*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/users*") Web.status=200 Web.http_method=GET by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_user_agent Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) AND NOT cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
n8n public API endpoint enumeration / credential-harvest fan-out from single source AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single source IP touching many distinct n8n /api/v1/ endpoints (workflows, users, credentials, executions, variables) within a short window — the harvesting pattern of an attacker validating a leaked token and inventorying everything it can reach. GitGuardian ran exactly this read-only enumeration against 896 reachable instances. Rationale: Uses the article's read-only validation-then-inventory behaviour and the concrete /api/v1/ endpoint namespace; distinct-endpoint fan-out from one source is far higher-fidelity than any single call and is what a token-validation pipeline looks like on the wire. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitguardian.com/n8n-security-encryption-key-compromise/
ATT&CKT1087 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An n8n SDK / API client performing a full sync that legitimately walks every endpoint
  • Backup or config-export tooling snapshotting workflows + credentials + variables
  • A developer manually exploring the API in Swagger/Postman
  • Migration script moving workflows between instances
  • Vulnerability scanner fingerprinting the API surface
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SrcIpAddr and the exact endpoint set; a burst that includes /api/v1/credentials + /api/v1/users + workflow reads is high-signal. Map to a known automation source or flag as unknown. 2) Contain: revoke API keys used from that IP, block the IP at the WAF, and force API-key expiry (n8n 1.78.0+ 30-day default) on all keys. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same token/IP into POST /api/v1/workflows (attacker creating a workflow to exercise stored credentials) and into any subsequent CVE-2025-68613 expression-injection payloads for host RCE.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has "/api/v1/"
| extend Endpoint = extract(@"(/api/v1/[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(Endpoint)
| summarize DistinctEndpoints=dcount(Endpoint), Endpoints=make_set(Endpoint, 25), Reqs=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctEndpoints >= 4   // 4+ distinct sensitive endpoints in 10m = harvest, not a single workflow call
| order by DistinctEndpoints desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(Web.url) as urls dc(Web.url) as distinct_urls from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/*" by Web.src _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rex field=urls max_match=0 "(?<endpoint>/api/v1/[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+)" | eval distinct_endpoints=mvcount(mvdedup(endpoint)) | where distinct_endpoints>=4 | sort - distinct_endpoints
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.url) as urls dc(Web.url) as distinct_urls from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/*" by Web.src _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rex field=urls max_match=0 "(?<endpoint>/api/v1/[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+)" | eval distinct_endpoints=mvcount(mvdedup(endpoint)) | where distinct_endpoints>=4 | sort - distinct_endpoints
n8n API key (X-N8N-API-KEY) exposed on command line or in Claude Code config on endpoint AIDelivery High
Hunts the secret-sprawl root cause: an n8n API JWT passed via the X-N8N-API-KEY header on a curl/process command line, or written into approved-command config such as .claude/settings.json / .claude/settings.local.json. The article shows Claude Code storing both the instance URL and API key inside an approved Bash(curl ... -H "X-N8N-API-KEY: eyJ...") entry that gets committed without .gitignore protection. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim X-N8N-API-KEY header string and the Claude Code Bash(curl ... -H "X-N8N-API-KEY: eyJ...") pattern; a raw n8n token on any command line is unambiguously a live secret and near-zero-noise, catching the exposure before it reaches a public commit. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitguardian.com/n8n-security-encryption-key-compromise/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer/admin legitimately calling their own n8n instance via curl during setup (the intended-but-risky pattern the article calls out)
  • CI/CD pipeline step that authenticates to n8n with the header inline
  • Claude Code or another AI agent executing an approved curl against n8n
  • Infrastructure automation (Ansible/Make) templating the header into a shell task
  • Local dev/test scripts against a throwaway n8n instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and extract the JWT after X-N8N-API-KEY; decode it (aud=public-api) to identify the target instance and jti, and check the iat/exp — pre-1.78.0 tokens often have no exp. 2) Contain: treat the token as compromised — revoke it in n8n, rotate N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY and downstream credentials, and scan the user's repos/commit history and .claude/settings*.json for the same value to prevent public exposure. 3) Hunt: search web-access logs for that token/instance being used from external IPs (UC1/UC2), and sweep other endpoints for X-N8N-API-KEY and N8N_API_KEY strings in files and shell history.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "X-N8N-API-KEY"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "X-N8N-API-KEY"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: n8n API Key Exposed on Command Line via X-N8N-API-KEY Header

description: Detects a process invoked with the n8n X-N8N-API-KEY authentication header on its command line, exposing a live n8n API token (secret sprawl).

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    category: process_creation

detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '

falsepositives:

Open VSX Removes 77 Malicious Evil Twin Extensions Exfiltrating Developer Data

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 13 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A cluster of 77 extensions on the Open VSX marketplace has been found to impersonate legitimate developer tools while transmitting information about the systems and development environments on which they were installed. The "evil twin" extensions were uploaded to the repository between July 26 and August 1, 2026, according to Manifold Security. The packages have been removed from Open VSX as of

Open VSX evil-twin extension exfil to mangorbit[.]com / npm-cache[.]com AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the campaign's hardcoded data-exfiltration infrastructure (mangorbit[.]com and its pulse/api/cb subdomains, plus npm-cache[.]com). All 77 malicious Open VSX extensions POST harvested developer/CI metadata to this domain, and the recon variant queries a DNS TXT record on it to fetch a fallback URL — so both A and TXT lookups are in scope. Rationale: mangorbit[.]com is the single hardcoded exfil domain shared by all 77 packages (registered 2026-07-15, 11 days before first upload) and npm-cache[.]com is a linked IOC; both are pure attacker infrastructure so any resolution is high-fidelity. Corroborated by BleepingComputer/Manifold recommending an outright block of mangorbit[.]com. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/77-open-vsx-extensions-found-harvesting-developer-info/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/open-vsx-removes-77-malicious-evil-twin.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected — mangorbit[.]com/npm-cache[.]com are dedicated attacker domains with no legitimate use
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonation of the extension inside the corporate estate
  • Threat-intel or blocklist validation tooling deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Passive DNS mirroring appliance replaying historical queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the InitiatingProcess (expect Code.exe / node.exe / a code-editor fork) that made the connection; pull the list of installed Open VSX/VS Code extensions on that host. 2) Contain: block mangorbit[.]com + npm-cache[.]com at egress/DNS, isolate the host, and remove any extension whose folder matches the 19 named evil-twin IDs. 3) Hunt: sweep all developer endpoints for the same domain resolutions and for extension folders versioned -0.0.1; rotate any Git/CI/cloud tokens that were readable from the affected workspaces.

Malicious Open VSX evil-twin extension install (named IDs, version 0.0.1) AIInstallation High
Detects on-disk installation of the campaign's evil-twin extensions by matching the 19 named recon extension IDs inside an editor extensions directory AND the tell-tale low version marker (-0.0.1). The attackers republish real extension names/namespaces through unrelated accounts at version 0.0.1 with a weaponised extension.js, so the ID+version pair separates the malicious twin from the legitimate package. Rationale: Uses the article's exact list of 19 named recon extension IDs plus the stated malicious version marker ("a low version number (e.g., 0.0.1)") scoped to editor extension directories, which cleanly separates the evil twin from the legitimately-named package. IDs and version behaviour corroborated by Manifold via BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/open-vsx-removes-77-malicious-evil-twin.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/77-open-vsx-extensions-found-harvesting-developer-info/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1176.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately publishing/pinning their own extension at genuine version 0.0.1 during local development (rare in a managed estate)
  • An offline VSIX sideload of a real same-named extension that coincidentally carries version 0.0.1
  • Backup/restore tooling re-materialising an old extensions folder
  • Security team pushing a benign test extension named 0.0.1 for pipeline validation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the extension folder version and publisher; open the bundled extension.js and check for calls to mangorbit[.]com or a status-bar 'anonymous usage metrics' string. 2) Contain: uninstall/quarantine the extension folder on the host and block mangorbit[.]com egress; snapshot the workspace for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 to see whether the extension already beaconed, enumerate the same 19 IDs across all developer endpoints, and rotate Git/CI/cloud tokens exposed in the affected workspaces.

ChainDrop npm preinstall dropper (setup.mjs / Bun runtime / Math_Symbol.js) AIInstallation High
Detects the ChainDrop / Mini Shai-Hulud worm's install-time dropper: an npm preinstall lifecycle hook that fetches a standalone Bun runtime and executes the obfuscated second stage. Anchors on the named artifacts setup.mjs (preinstall dropper) and Math_Symbol.js (second stage) appearing in a node/npm process command line. Rationale: Anchors on the ChainDrop worm's named install artifacts — setup.mjs preinstall dropper and Math_Symbol.js second stage — plus the article's stated behaviour of downloading a standalone Bun runtime executed from an npm preinstall hook. Artifact names corroborated by Microsoft, Expel and SecurityWeek write-ups of ChainDrop. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://expel.com/blog/chaindrop-the-mini-shai-hulud-npm-worms-latest-wave-hits-keyv-and-cacheable/ • https://www.securityweek.com/over-400-npm-packages-infected-in-chaindrop-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project that genuinely ships a file named setup.mjs in a preinstall hook (uncommon; verify the file contents)
  • A developer intentionally installing the Bun runtime via npm for a Bun-based project
  • CI images that pre-bake Bun during npm install for legitimate builds
  • Security researchers detonating a ChainDrop sample in an approved lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and the npm package name/version that triggered the preinstall hook; hash the bundled second stage and check against the article SHA256s. 2) Contain: kill node/bun processes, isolate the host, invalidate the npm token used on that machine, and pull the package from any internal registry mirror. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts that installed the same package versions (2,244 artifacts across ~450 packages), check for stolen GitHub/AWS/npm credential reuse, and pivot to UC4 for .claude/.vscode persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
   or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "preinstall" and ProcessCommandLine has "bun")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe") and FileName =~ "bun.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
   or (ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm-cli.js") and CommandLine has "bun" and CommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop persistence via .claude / .vscode autostart injection by node/bun AIInstallation Medium
Detects the ChainDrop worm planting autostart hooks in .claude and .vscode config directories to reach developers and AI coding agents that clone the poisoned source. Flags node/bun/npm processes writing JSON config into a repo-local .claude or .vscode folder — a developer-to-developer infection path Socket flagged as new to this Shai-Hulud descendant. Rationale: Grounds on the article's explicit statement that the worm 'plants autostart hooks in .claude and .vscode to reach developers and AI coding agents who clone the source', scoping to node/bun/npm as the writing process to cut noise. Behaviour corroborated by Socket and Microsoft ChainDrop analyses. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/supply-chain-attacks/mini-shai-hulud • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/
ATT&CKT1176.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate project scaffolding tools (create-react-app, nx, generators) that write .vscode/settings.json or tasks.json during setup
  • A developer or the Claude/VS Code tooling itself writing .claude or .vscode config on first workspace open
  • Formatter/linter extensions persisting workspace settings via a node helper
  • Monorepo tooling regenerating .vscode config across packages
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("create-react-app","nx generate","yeoman","@vscode/vsce") or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written .claude/.vscode file and inspect for autostart commands (tasks with runOn/preLaunch, MCP servers, or shell payloads) rather than benign editor settings; correlate the writing npm package/version. 2) Contain: revert the injected config in the repo, block outbound to ChainDrop C2 (npm-cache[.]com), and rotate GitHub credentials that could push the change. 3) Hunt: search git history for committed .claude/.vscode changes across cloned repos, check for the setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js dropper (UC3) on the same hosts, and review CI for auto-triggered agent runs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","bun.exe","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\", @"\.vscode\")
| where FileName in~ ("settings.json","tasks.json","mcp.json","extensions.json","launch.json")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","bun.exe","npm.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.claude\", @"\.vscode\", "/.claude/", "/.vscode/")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("settings.json","tasks.json","mcp.json","extensions.json","launch.json")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
